slides.text:
A template is text with holes. The `text/template` package fills the holes with data and writes the result: emails, reports, config files, generated code.

The snippet is pseudo code: a template, its data and what comes out.
slides.code:
template: Hello, {{.name}}!
data:     name = Ana
result:   Hello, Ana!

slides.text:
A hole is an **action**, written between `{{` and `}}`. Everything outside the actions is copied to the output as it is.

Inside an action, the dot `.` stands for the data you give the template.

`text/template` writes plain text and does no escaping. For HTML pages the standard library has `html/template`, with the same syntax and safe output.

You will build and run templates, read values from maps, handle errors and shape the output. Conditions, loops and functions come in the next module.
Using a template takes two steps. **Parse** turns the text into a template and checks its syntax. **Execute** fills the holes with data and writes the result to a writer.
slides.code:
t, err := template.New("n").Parse(s)
err = t.Execute(w, data)

slides.text:
The writer is anything that can receive text: the terminal, a file, a network connection. The data is any value, and inside the template the dot is that value.

A map gives the template named values: `.name` reads the key `name`.

slides.text:
With a map as data, `.key` reads one entry. When an entry is itself a map, the keys chain with more dots.

The snippet is pseudo code.

A key that is not in the map is not an error by default: the hole prints a placeholder text.

The `Option` method changes this. `missingkey=zero` prints the zero value of the map's element type, and `missingkey=error` makes `Execute` fail.

Two things can fail. **Parse** fails on broken syntax, such as a hole that never closes. **Execute** fails on data problems, such as a strict missing key.

Both return an `error`, and `Must` turns a parse error into a panic.

slides.text:
Text around a hole is copied exactly, spaces and newlines included. A dash inside the braces trims it: `{{-` removes the whitespace before the hole and `-}}` removes the whitespace after it.

The snippet is pseudo code.

A comment is `{{/* text */}}`. It prints nothing. It explains the template to whoever edits it next.

Trim markers work with comments too, with spaces around the comment: `{{- /* note */ -}}`.

`{{define "name"}}...{{end}}` stores a block of text under a name. `{{template "name" data}}` runs it, with that data as its dot.

A template can hold many named blocks, and `ExecuteTemplate` runs one of them by name.
